author: Newsweek
title: VA Benefits Update: Court Fight for Trans Veterans Retirement Plays Out
text:
The case was argued Tuesday and will decide whether the Air Force unlawfully canceled early retirement approvals.
A group of 17 transgender veterans and service members is fighting in federal court to restore retirement benefits they say were improperly revoked under theThe case was argued Tuesday in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims and will decide whether the Air Force unlawfully canceled“The Air Force abruptly reversed that promise without cause — ripping away the financial support and benefits that these service members earned, and their families were counting on,” the plaintiffs said in a statement from their attorneys.
The lawsuit could determine whether affected service members receive military retirement pensions and health benefits they earned from their lengthy careers in the military. For veterans nearing retirement, the outcome will also likely carry significant financial consequences. Currently, the plaintiffs stand to lose substantial lifetime retirement income and health care benefits after serving for more than 15 years. , was brought by 17 transgender service members and veterans who served in the Air Force and Space Force.
According to court filings, each had at least 15 years of military service when they sought early retirement after the enactment of the Trump administration's transgender troop ban. The plaintiffs said that the Air Force approved their retirements under the Temporary Early Retirement Authority program before later rescinding those approvals. The lawsuit alleges those retirement orders were legally authorized and should not have been reversed.
Among the lead plaintiffs is former Air Force Master Sergeant Logan Ireland, an Afghanistan veteran who says the government's actions stripped away benefits he and other service members had planned their futures around.
“I raised my hand and served my country honorably for 15 years, including a deployment to Afghanistan,” Ireland said as reported by military news organization Stars and Stripes. “Long-serving service members and their families build their lives around the promise of earned retirement. When that promise is revoked, it does not just affect a paycheck, it affects housing, health care, family stability, and a lifetime of financial security.
”The hearing this week focused on the government's motion to dismiss the case. Federal attorneys argued that the Court of Federal Claims lacks jurisdiction over the dispute, while attorneys for the plaintiffs contend the court can hear claims involving military pay and retirement benefits. Most at issue is President Trump's January 2025 executive order reversing the Biden administration policy that allowed transgender troops to serve openly.
The order stated that service members expressing a gender identity different from their biological sex could not meet the standards required for military service. Under subsequent Defense Department guidance, troops with a diagnosis or history of gender dysphoria became subject to separation from military service.
“Consistent with the military mission and longstanding policy, expressing a false ‘gender identity’ divergent from an individual’s sex cannot satisfy the rigorous standards necessary for military service,” the order said. The specific retirement benefits dispute emerged after affected service members sought to leave through early retirement rather than face separation under the new policy. Plaintiffs said they received approved retirement orders before those approvals were ultimately withdrawn.
“The plaintiffs claim they had more than 15 years of honorable service, were approved for early retirement, and then were told they would instead be separated without those pensions or lifetime TRICARE access, a loss that could add up to millions of dollars over a lifetime,” Alex Beene, a financial literacy instructor for the University of Tennessee at Martin, told“If benefits can be rescinded after the fact, it raises major questions about whether service members can rely on promises made to them when policy changes. ”The retirement benefits lawsuit is one of several ongoing legal challenges involving transgender military service.
In June, a federal appeals court concluded the Trump administration's transgender military policy was likely unconstitutional and allowed certain active-duty plaintiffs to remain in service while litigation continues. But broader legal disputes over the policy remain unresolved.
However, for this specific case, the stakes are more about whether the government can take back promised retirement benefits, said Michael Ryan, a finance expert and the founder of MichaelRyanMoney.com.
“It's not about whether they should've been allowed to serve. It's about whether the government can dangle earned retirement, get people to sign up for it, then reverse course without consequence,” Ryan toldThe Court of Federal Claims must first decide whether to grant the government's motion to dismiss or allow the lawsuit to proceed.
If the court finds it has jurisdiction, the case would move forward to consider the plaintiffs' claims that the Air Force unlawfully canceled approved early retirements and deprived them of retirement pay and benefits. If they win, it says something simple but massive. Federal promises can't be revoked just because the politics changed. Right now, service members approved for early retirement might not be as secure as they think when an administration flips,” Ryan said.
“This case could force the government to honor commitments or pay the damage. ”
